subject: Core inflation cooled. Expectations did not.
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a mortgage renewal coming up, or you are choosing between a fixed and a variable rate, the Bank of Canada's October 28 decision got harder to read yesterday. Three releases landed on Monday and they do not agree with each other.

## The headline was gasoline

Statistics Canada reported on Monday that the Consumer Price Index rose 3.1 per cent in September from a year earlier, up from 3.0 per cent in August, and 0.1 per cent on the month. Reuters had polled economists expecting 3.2 per cent, so this came in soft. Gasoline is doing almost all of the lifting, up 27.8 per cent from a year ago. Take gasoline out and prices rose 2.2 per cent, down from 2.4 per cent in August. The Bank's **core inflation** gauges, which discard the most extreme price moves each month to find the underlying trend, both eased too: CPI-trim slipped to 1.8 per cent from 1.9, and CPI-median to 1.9 per cent from 2.0. CIBC's Avery Shenfeld told the CBC that "we have inflation in gasoline prices, which every Canadian already knew, but we don't have a lot of inflation anywhere else." On the report itself, he is right.

## The Bank's own surveys say something colder

That same morning the Bank published its third-quarter Business Outlook Survey and its Canadian Survey of Consumer Expectations. Canadians now expect inflation of 3.91 per cent five years out, the highest that reading has been since the second quarter of 2022, up from 3.39 per cent in the spring. One year out they expect 4.03 per cent, and their spending plans got worse from levels that were already weak. Among firms seeing bigger cost increases than usual, more than 40 per cent intend **pass-through**, meaning they will raise their own prices to cover those costs, within a year, and roughly a quarter said they already have. The business outlook indicator did improve, to -0.33 from -0.38. Watch the dates, though. Interviews ran from August 6 to September 2, and about three quarters finished before Canada and the United States broke off trade talks on August 21. The Bank said expectations climbed after that.

## Why the expectations number beats the print

A central bank can look through a gasoline spike. It cannot look through households budgeting for 4 per cent, because that is how a temporary price shock hardens into a wage and pricing habit. Tiff Macklem has already named his trigger, telling reporters that if oil prices stay around US$100, "we expect inflation to gradually drift up from where it is today: three per cent." Pulling the other way is a shrinking job market. Statistics Canada counted 68,000 jobs lost in September with unemployment near 6.5 per cent, and RBC's Abbey Xu noted employment fell in August too. The policy rate sits at 2.25 per cent. So Macklem picks between raising rates into a weakening labour market or sitting still while the public quietly re-anchors higher. TD's Leslie Preston reads the data as support for holding through year end. Oxford Economics' Michael Davenport called the print a tad softer than he expected, then called it "a very close call."

## The takeaway

I would stop treating October 28 as a live question about a hike and start treating it as a hold with hard language attached. The sentence to hunt for in the statement is the one on inflation expectations, since it tells you whether 2027 brings cuts or the opposite. Keep one eye on oil, because Macklem handed you US$100 as a number to watch and that beats parsing a whole CPI release. If you are renewing inside six months, the softer core measures are your argument for shopping a variable rate instead of signing the first fixed offer your lender hands you.
